lessons.title: Reading: finding information
lessons.keyIdea: Retrieval answers are in the text. Find the right paragraph, then read it carefully.

sections.heading: Skim and scan
sections.body: Skim to get the gist of each paragraph. Scan for key words from the question (names, numbers, dates).

sections.heading: Use the question words
sections.body: If a question says “according to paragraph 3”, the answer is there — not anywhere else. Give exactly the number of points asked for.

sections.heading: Summarising
sections.body: A summary gives the main points in your own words, leaving out small details.

workedExamples.question: “Give two materials used to make bee hotels.”
steps: Scan for “bamboo”, “wood”, “straws”.
Paragraph 2 lists bamboo canes, paper straws and drilled wood.
Write two of them.

commonMistakes: Answering from memory instead of the text.
Giving one point when two are asked for.
Copying a whole paragraph instead of the answer.
lessons.examTip: Underline key words in the question before you look back at the text.

lessons.title: Reading: inference and interpretation
lessons.keyIdea: Inference is reading between the lines: use clues in the text to work out what is not said directly.

sections.heading: Clues
sections.body: Look at what characters do, say and notice. Clutching a bag and checking a watch repeatedly suggests worry.

sections.heading: Point – Evidence – Explain
sections.body: Make your point, quote a short piece of evidence, then explain how it shows your point: “Amira is anxious. She checks her watch ‘again, then again’, which shows she is worried the bus will not come.”

workedExamples.question: How does the grandmother feel when Jonah returns?
steps: She is waiting on the slipway in her nightgown.
She wraps her coat around him without speaking.
Her actions show relief and love.

commonMistakes: Retelling the story instead of explaining.
Making a guess with no evidence.
Using long quotations — keep them short.
lessons.examTip: For 2-mark inference questions, always give a point AND evidence.

lessons.title: Language analysis
lessons.keyIdea: Writers choose words for effect. Name the technique, then explain what it makes the reader think or feel.

sections.heading: Techniques
sections.body: Simile: comparison with like/as. Metaphor: says one thing is another. Personification: human qualities for non-human things. Alliteration: repeated starting sounds. Rhetorical question: a question for effect.

sections.heading: Explaining effect
sections.body: Do not stop at the name. Say what picture it creates: “the sky turned the colour of a bruise” suggests dark, threatening clouds and hints that Jonah is in danger.

workedExamples.question: Explain “the engine coughed”.
steps: Technique: personification.
Engines cannot cough; people cough when ill.
It suggests the engine is struggling and might fail.
workedExamples.answer: It shows the engine is unreliable, adding tension.

commonMistakes: Naming a technique without explaining its effect.
Writing “it makes it more interesting” — be specific.
Confusing simile and metaphor.
lessons.examTip: Zoom in on one word: what are its connotations?

lessons.title: Text organisation and purpose
lessons.keyIdea: Every text has a purpose and an audience, and its structure helps it achieve that purpose.

sections.heading: Purpose and audience
sections.body: Is the text trying to inform, persuade, instruct, entertain or recount? Who is it written for?

sections.heading: Structural features
sections.body: Headings, paragraphs, chronological order, short paragraphs for emphasis, an opening hook and a concluding paragraph that sums up or speaks to the reader.

sections.heading: Fiction structure
sections.body: Writers build tension with short sentences, cliffhangers and pacing, and end with a resolution or a twist.

workedExamples.question: Why is paragraph 2 of “The Audition” one sentence long?
steps: It is much shorter than the paragraphs around it.
It stands out to the reader.
It emphasises Leila’s sudden panic.

commonMistakes: Describing what happens instead of how the text is organised.
Confusing purpose (why) with audience (who).
lessons.examTip: Look at the beginning and the end of the text — they often show the structure most clearly.

lessons.title: Vocabulary
lessons.keyIdea: Work out word meanings from context and from word parts.

sections.heading: Context clues
sections.body: Read the whole sentence: “The scientist was meticulous, checking every measurement three times” → meticulous means very careful.

sections.heading: Word parts
sections.body: Prefixes change meaning (un-, dis-, mis-, im-, re-). Suffixes change word class (-ment, -ness, -ly, -ful). Roots carry meaning (aqua = water, port = carry).

sections.heading: Precise choices
sections.body: Choose the word that fits exactly: “trudged” is more precise than “walked” for a tired soldier.

workedExamples.question: What does “illegible” mean in “His writing was so messy it was illegible”?
steps: il- means not.
“legible” means able to be read.
The sentence talks about messy writing.

commonMistakes: Choosing a word that looks similar instead of one that means the same.
Ignoring the sentence around the word.
lessons.examTip: Swap your answer into the sentence. If it still makes sense, it is probably right.

lessons.title: Grammar
lessons.keyIdea: Grammar is how words work together. Keep tenses consistent and make subjects and verbs agree.

sections.heading: Word classes
sections.body: Noun (thing), verb (action/being), adjective (describes a noun), adverb (describes a verb), preposition (position/time), conjunction (joins clauses), pronoun (replaces a noun).

sections.heading: Tense and agreement
sections.body: Keep the same tense unless the time changes. Singular subjects take singular verbs: “Neither of the boys was ready.”

sections.heading: Active and passive
sections.body: Active: “The ball broke the window.” Passive: “The window was broken (by the ball).” The passive puts the focus on what the action happened to.

workedExamples.question: Change to the passive: “The chef cooked the meal.”
steps: Object becomes the subject: the meal.
Use was/were + past participle: was cooked.
Add “by the chef”.
workedExamples.answer: The meal was cooked by the chef.

commonMistakes: Switching tenses mid-sentence.
Using “less” for countable things.
Confusing adjectives and adverbs.
lessons.examTip: Read your sentence aloud in your head — mistakes often sound wrong.

lessons.title: Punctuation and spelling
lessons.keyIdea: Punctuation makes meaning clear. Learn the rules for apostrophes, speech and the colon family.

sections.heading: Apostrophes
sections.body: Contraction: they’re = they are, it’s = it is. Possession: the dog’s bowl (one dog), the girls’ room (several girls). Never use an apostrophe just to make a plural.

sections.heading: Speech
sections.body: “Are you coming?” asked Sam. The spoken words and their punctuation go inside the speech marks. Start a new line for a new speaker.

sections.heading: Colons, semicolons, brackets and dashes
sections.body: A colon introduces a list or explanation. A semicolon joins two related complete sentences. Brackets and dashes add extra information.

workedExamples.question: Punctuate: its time to go said mum
steps: “It’s” = it is, so it needs an apostrophe.
Speech marks around the spoken words, with a comma inside.
Capital letter for the start and full stop at the end.

commonMistakes: Its / it’s confusion.
Putting the question mark outside the speech marks.
Using a comma to join two sentences.
lessons.examTip: Check every apostrophe: can you expand it, or does it show ownership? If neither, delete it.

lessons.title: Sentence construction and editing
lessons.keyIdea: Vary your sentences and join ideas correctly so your writing is clear and interesting.

sections.heading: Sentence types
sections.body: Simple: one main clause. Compound: two main clauses joined with and/but/or/so. Complex: a main clause plus a subordinate clause (because, when, although, if).

sections.heading: Avoiding comma splices
sections.body: “It was raining, we stayed in” is wrong. Fix it with a conjunction (“so”), a full stop or a semicolon.

sections.heading: Editing
sections.body: Check capital letters, full stops, verb agreement, tense and repetition. Cut unnecessary words and choose precise vocabulary.

workedExamples.question: Combine: “The fox was hungry. The fox crept towards the henhouse.”
steps: Avoid repeating “the fox”.
Turn “hungry” into an adjective.
workedExamples.answer: The hungry fox crept towards the henhouse.

commonMistakes: Joining sentences with a comma alone.
Starting too many sentences with “Then”.
Repeating the same word.
lessons.examTip: Begin some sentences with a fronted adverbial (“Without a sound,”) — and remember the comma.
